summary: Defines a MIB module for managing pseudowire edge-to-edge services carried over a general packet switched network, giving network management tools a standard way to model and monitor them.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5601 defines the SNMP managed objects for pseudowires, the emulated connections a carrier runs over a packet network. One table holds the settings and status that are the same for every pseudowire, and other modules hold what depends on the service being emulated and on the packet network carrying it, all tied together by one index. The RFC also says how rows are created, what the status values mean, and how the objects should be protected.

questions: how to manage pseudowires with snmp
what tables are in the pw mib
subtitle: The SNMP objects that let a manager configure and watch the pseudowires a carrier runs over its packet network.

tldr.problem: A carrier runs many pseudowires over a packet network, and each one has settings and counters that need to be inspected and sometimes changed. Without managed objects, there is no standard way to do that, and the same pseudowire appears differently depending on which packet network carries it.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines two MIB modules. PW-STD-MIB holds the settings and status that are the same for every kind of pseudowire, in a table indexed by a pwIndex that identifies one virtual connection. Service-specific and packet-network-specific modules hold the rest, and are tied to the main table by that same index, so a manager can walk from a pseudowire to the tunnel carrying it and the service it emulates.
tldr.outcome: The result is a common management layer for pseudowires whatever the emulated service and whatever the packet network underneath. The RFC also says how rows may be created and changed, what a pseudowire's status values mean, and that SNMPv3 with its access control and user-based security must be used with it.

facts.label: Historical entries
facts.value: 96 fifteen-minute entries for 24 hours, 30 one-day entries for a month

today: RFC 5601 is a Proposed Standard from July 2009 and is neither obsoleted nor updated. It defines the generic pseudowire MIB, PW-STD-MIB, whose object identifier sits under the transmission subtree because a pseudowire may also appear in the standard interface table, and the IANA-PWE3-MIB module of shared textual conventions. The packet-network-specific modules that build on it are in other documents, for example RFC 5602 for MPLS.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base for use with network management protocols in the Internet community. In particular, it defines a MIB module that can be used to manage pseudowire services for transmission over a packet switched network. It provides generic management of pseudowires that is common to all the types of packet network and pseudowire service defined by the IETF Pseudowire Emulation Edge-to-Edge working group.

Managed objects are accessed through a virtual information store, the Management Information Base, and MIB objects are generally accessed through the Simple Network Management Protocol. The objects in this MIB are defined using the mechanisms of the Structure of Management Information, and the module is compliant with SMIv2, described in RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580.
sections.plainLanguage: The document defines the settings and counters a network manager can read and change for a pseudowire, in a form that is the same whatever the service being emulated and whatever the packet network carrying it.

sections.title: Overview: Three Kinds of MIB Module
sections.content:
The PWE3 MIB module architecture provides a layered modular model into which any supported emulated service can be connected to any supported packet network type. This particular MIB module provides the glue for mapping the emulated service onto the native packet network service. Defining a pseudowire emulated service therefore requires the use of at least three kinds of MIB module.

The first type is a service-specific module, which depends on the emulated signal type, and these are defined in other documents. The second type is the module in this memo, PW-STD-MIB, which configures the general parameters of the pseudowire that are common to all types of emulated service and packet network type. The third type is a packet-network-specific module, with a different module for each type of packet network. Those modules associate the pseudowire with one or more tunnels that carry the service over the packet network, and they are also defined in other documents.
sections.plainLanguage: A pseudowire needs three sets of managed objects: one for the service it fakes, one for the tunnel that carries it, and this one, which holds what is the same in every case. The pwIndex links them together.

sections.title: The Six Tables
sections.content:
The MIB module consists of six tables.

The pwTable holds the generic configuration and status monitoring objects that are common to all service types and packet network types. The pwPerfCurrentTable holds pseudowire statistics for the current 15-minute period, and the pwPerfIntervalTable holds statistics for historical intervals, usually 96 15-minute entries to cover a 24-hour period. The pwPerf1DayIntervalTable holds statistics for historical intervals accumulated per day, usually 30 one-day entries to cover a monthly period.

The last two tables are for reverse lookups. The pwIndexMappingTable enables the reverse mapping of the unique pseudowire parameters, the peer IP address, the pseudowire type and the pseudowire ID, to the pwIndex. The pwGenFecIndexMappingTable enables the reverse mapping of the unique pseudowire parameters used in generic FEC signalling, the group attachment ID, the local attachment ID and the peer attachment ID, to the pwIndex.

Inside the main table, a row represents a pseudowire virtual connection across the packet network, and it is indexed by the pwIndex, which uniquely identifies a single connection. The row carries the pseudowire type, its owner, the packet network type, the setup and holding priorities, the peer address and the identifiers used to signal it, the control word preferences, the fragmentation and retention settings, the inbound and outbound labels, names and timestamps, the administrative and operational status, and the counters.
sections.plainLanguage: There is one main table, one row per pseudowire, and three tables of counters: what has happened in the last quarter of an hour, what happened in each of the last ninety-six quarter hours, and what happened on each of the last thirty days. The last two tables let a manager go from the numbers that identify a pseudowire back to its index.

sections.title: How Rows Are Created and Changed
sections.content:
An entry in the pwTable must exist for all pseudowire types, ATM, frame relay, Ethernet and SONET among them, and the table holds the generic parameters related to the creation and monitoring of the pseudowire. A conceptual row can be created in three ways.

The operator can create a row when configuring the node for a new service. The agent must support this mode, and must use it when creating a non-signalled, manually assigned pseudowire. The agent may create a row if a signalling message has been received from a peer node with signalling identification parameters that are not already known to the local node, that is, when there is no related entry created by the operator with matching parameters; this mode is optional. The agent may also create a row automatically because of some auto-discovery application, or based on configuration done through non-SNMP applications; this mode is optional as well. In these last two cases the agent then creates the matching rows in the locally supported performance tables and reverse-mapping tables.

The read-create objects in a row fall into three categories. Some must not be changed after row activation, because they define the basic properties of the pseudowire, such as its type and its destination. Some may be changed when the pseudowire is defined as not active, which means its row status is notInService or notReady, or its administrative status is down; a change of these objects involves re-signalling the pseudowire or might affect traffic, so the operator who needs to change one of them for an active row can either set the row status to notInService or set the administrative status to down, and signalling or traffic is initiated again when the row status is set to active or the administrative status to up or testing. The rest may be changed at any time.

The RFC also says that manual entries in this table should be preserved after a reboot, and that the agent must ensure their integrity. If the entries of a row are found to be inconsistent after a reboot, the operational status of that pseudowire must be declared as notPresent.
sections.plainLanguage: A row can be put there by an operator, by the agent when a peer signals a new pseudowire, or by the agent on its own. Some of the values in a row are fixed once it is in service, and others can only be changed while the pseudowire is out of service, because changing them re-signals it.

sections.title: Relations to Other MIB Modules
sections.content:
Rows in the other PWE3 modules are tied to the main table by the common pwIndex. Based on the packet network type defined for the pseudowire, a row is created in the corresponding packet-network-specific module, for example the MPLS one, and associated with the pwTable by that index. Based on the pseudowire type, a row is created in the corresponding service-specific module, for example the circuit emulation one, and associated in the same way.

Unless all the necessary entries in the applicable tables have been created and all the parameters have been consistently configured in those tables, signalling cannot be performed from the local node, and the operational status object should report notPresent.

The relation to the standard interface MIB is different. A pseudowire is in general not an ifIndex on its own, for reasons of agent scalability, and it is typically associated through the PWE3 modules to an ifIndex for the thing it is emulating. That ifIndex may represent a physical entity, for example a pseudowire emulating a SONET path as in circuit emulation over packet, in which case the pseudowire itself is not an ifIndex and the service-specific module associates the pseudowire with the ifIndex of the path to be emulated. In some cases the pseudowire is associated with an ifIndex that represents a virtual interface, as in Virtual Private LAN Service, where the pseudowire emulates a logical interface of a logical bridge. An exception may exist in some implementations where it is convenient to manage the pseudowire as an ifIndex in the interface table, and a special ifType for a pseudowire virtual interface, 246, is used in that case. When the pseudowire is managed as an ifIndex, it should by default not be stacked, that is, that ifIndex should not be layered above the packet network tunnel index, the attachment circuit index, or the interface carrying the attachment circuit.
sections.plainLanguage: The index of a pseudowire row is the link to the other tables, so a manager can follow it to the tunnel and to the emulated service. The pseudowire is usually not listed in the standard interface table, because that table would grow too large; it is linked to the interface it emulates instead.

sections.title: PW Notifications
sections.content:
This MIB module includes notifications for a pseudowire entering the up or down state, in accordance with the guidelines for interface notifications. Implementers should be aware that in many systems it is desired to correlate notifications, so that a notification is not emitted if a notification from a higher level, such as from ports or tunnels, is already in effect. Specifically for pseudowires, it is anticipated that most network equipment failures turn into a lowerLayerDown state at the pseudowire level, where a notification has already been emitted from a higher level.

When a pseudowire is represented as an ifIndex, it is recommended that pseudowire notifications be turned off, to avoid duplication with the ifIndex status change notifications.
sections.plainLanguage: The module reports a pseudowire going up or down, but in most equipment a failure is already reported by the port or the tunnel below it, so the RFC suggests not reporting it twice.

sections.title: An Example of Using the Modules
sections.content:
The RFC works through an example that sets up a circuit emulation pseudowire over an MPLS packet switched network, using an MPLS traffic engineering tunnel and LDP for service setup. The example is not meant to illustrate every part of the MIB, but is an aid to understanding some of the key concepts, and it is meant to be read after going through the MIB itself.

In the main table the example fills in the pseudowire index, the type set to circuit emulation, the owner, the packet network type set to MPLS, the setup and holding priorities, the inbound mode, the peer address type and address, the pseudowire ID and the local group ID. It then sets the control word preference, with a comment that it is ignored for circuit emulation, the local interface MTU and interface string settings, the capability advertisement setting, with a comment that the switch does not support status reporting to the peer, and the remote group ID, with a comment that it will be received by the signalling protocol.

The example is continued in the memo describing the circuit emulation module and in the memo describing the MPLS module, which cover the operations in the service-specific and the packet-network-specific modules.
sections.plainLanguage: The example fills in one row of the main table for a circuit emulation pseudowire over MPLS, showing how the pieces fit together: the type, the peer, the priorities, the identifiers the signalling will use, and the settings that say how the control word and the status reporting should work.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This MIB module is potentially useful for monitoring pseudowire-capable provider edge devices, and it can also be used to configure some of its objects. Anything that can be configured can be configured incorrectly, with potentially disastrous results.

A number of the managed objects have a read-write or read-create access clause and may be considered sensitive or vulnerable in some network environments, and support for SET operations in a non-secure environment without proper protection can have a negative effect on network operations. The main table contains the objects that configure pseudowire parameters on a provider edge device, so unauthorized access to them could result in disruption of traffic on the network. The two objects that control the reports from the network element to the management system are called out as well, because unauthorized access to them could disrupt configuration and status change reporting and give a mis-view of the network conditions. The RFC says that stronger mechanisms such as SNMPv3 security should be considered where possible, and specifically that SNMPv3 view-based access control and the user-based security model must be used with any version 3 agent that implements this MIB module. Administrators should consider whether read access to these objects should be allowed, since read access may be undesirable in certain circumstances.

Some of the readable objects may also be sensitive, so it is important to control even GET and NOTIFY access to them and possibly to encrypt their values when they are sent over the network with SNMP. The tables concerned show the pseudowire connectivity topology and its performance characteristics, so an administrator who does not want to reveal that information should treat them as sensitive.

SNMP versions prior to SNMPv3 did not include adequate security, and even if the network itself is secure, for example by using IPsec, there is still no control over who on that network is allowed to read or change the objects in this module. The RFC therefore recommends the security features of the SNMPv3 framework, including full support for its cryptographic mechanisms for authentication and privacy, does not recommend deploying earlier SNMP versions, and leaves it to the operator to configure the SNMP entity so that it gives access only to the principals that have legitimate rights to read or change the objects.
sections.plainLanguage: Writing to the wrong object in this MIB can break live traffic, so the RFC insists on SNMPv3 with its access control and user-based security, and it warns that reading the tables reveals the shape of the network and how busy each pseudowire is.

viz.caption: THE OPERATIONAL STATUS OF A PSEUDOWIRE

items.label: down
items.desc: The pseudowire is not carrying traffic, because of a fault reported locally or by the peer.

items.label: notPresent
items.desc: The necessary entries in the other tables have not been created or configured, so signalling cannot be performed from this node.

items.label: lowerLayerDown
items.desc: The only reason the pseudowire is not up is that the tunnel or physical layer below it is down.
